title: Reintegration Offers to Serb and Croat Communities
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds, Vol. II (CIA, 2002), 1993-94 RBiH diplomatic posture chronology
content:
By the close of autumn 1993 the Sarajevo Presidency confronted a foreclosed diplomatic landscape. The May assembly rejection of Vance-Owen at Pale and the 29 September assembly rejection of Owen-Stoltenberg had killed both internationally brokered partition frameworks. Roughly 70 percent of pre-war Bosnia lay outside Sarajevo's effective control: the Krajina, Posavina, eastern Herzegovina, and the Drina valley under the VRS; western Herzegovina and the central-Bosnian pockets under the HVO.

The Presidency's posture toward the populations and territories it did not control was a defining political choice. Izetbegović's government had sustained a maximalist claim to a unitary, multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina across every diplomatic round — a claim that the embargo-starved ARBiH could not enforce on the ground. The question of autumn 1993 was whether to keep pressing that claim by force, or to offer the Serb and Croat communities a negotiated reintegration on terms short of unitary restoration.

The Balkan Battlegrounds chronology records Sarajevo holding the maximalist territorial line through Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg, the Contact Group plan, and Washington. The Presidency framed reintegration not as a concession of partition but as the reconstitution of the pre-war state — a framing that constrained how far it could go toward federation or autonomy offers without appearing to ratify the war's territorial outcomes.

The posture recorded here governs whether Sarajevo entered the 1994-95 endgame as an offensive claimant to the whole country, or as a negotiator prepared to trade unitary restoration for a durable settlement.
